newsitem.title: USA: Park-Ohio to acquire Arden Industries for $42 million.
newsitem.headline: Park-Ohio to acquire Arden Industries for $42 million.

text.p: Park-Ohio Industries Inc. said Tuesday it will pay $42 million to acquire Arden Industries Inc.,adding to what one analyst said is already the largest U.S. contractor for nuts and bolts for large manufacturers.

The deal values St. Paul, Minn.-based Arden Industries, a distributor of specialty and standard fasteners to the industrial market, at $6 a share. Arden's stock gained 31.25 cents to $5.6875 and Park-Ohio rose $1.6875 to $14.50, both on Nasdaq.

"The acquisition of Arden is a further commitment to our RB&W logistics business, which had sales of $151 million in 1996," said Edward Crawford, chief executive officer of Cleveland-based diversified manufacturer and logistics company Park-Ohio said. "This bolt-on transaction will open new areas for our products and strengthen current operations."
Arden had revenues of $87.5 million in the fiscal year ended June 30, 1996.

The deal has been approved by both companies' boards of directors but is still subject to other conditions, including satisfactory completion of Park-Ohio's diligence process and expiration of waiting periods under federal antitrust law.
One analyst said the antitrust review should not scuttle the deal because Arden and Park-Ohio generally operate in different parts of the country.
"They will have to go through the antitrust routine, but I think that they will not have any material issues there," said Alan Dorsey, analyst at Value Investing Partners Inc.

Dorsey said he expected the deal to be neutral to earnings for about a year. But he also said the fastener logistics business could grow revenues at 15-20 percent in the long term, with manufacturers willing to pay a premium not to have to worry about a lack of bolts and washers shutting down an entire production line.

"This service RB&W provides has tremendous growth over the next 5-10 years," Dorsey said. "They do the buying and ordering of bolts for large equipment makers, from refrigerators to trucks. If you run out of one kind of nut or washer, it can stop your entire production line and that's not a problem (manufacturers) want to have."
